name: ACH, stablecoin, and digital-asset laundering methods

attribution.legal_posture: Official U.S. government aggregate or risk-assessment finding. Underlying pending case summaries remain allegations where applicable

caveats: The case narratives summarize DOJ actions; repetition adds chronology rather than additional cases.
The assessment mixes Treasury risk analysis with summaries of allegations in pending or unresolved legal proceedings; legal posture must remain explicit.
The document gives March 2026; publication day remains unreported.
The NPFRA discusses ACH accounts, Malaysian documents, chain hopping, token swapping, NFTs, and commingling in the context of the $7.74 million forfeiture and four-worker theft cases.

statements: Treasury says that in 2025 North Korean IT workers in Russia sought ACH-enabled accounts at U.S. and other Western financial institutions using fraudulent U.S. identification documents so they could more readily receive direct-deposit payments from U.S. clients.

Treasury assesses that U.S. digital-asset service providers face substantial risk of unknowingly employing DPRK IT workers and notes that IT-worker salaries are remitted in digital assets, particularly stablecoins.

In summarizing the already-known $7.74 million civil-forfeiture matter, Treasury specifies laundering techniques including fictitious accounts, small structured transfers, chain hopping, token swapping, NFT purchases, U.S.-based online accounts, and commingling before proceeds were sent toward the DPRK.

In summarizing the already-known four-worker digital-asset theft case, Treasury states that exchange accounts controlled by DPRK nationals but held in alias names were opened using fraudulent Malaysian identification documents.
